title: How One Agent Stopped an Entire Company
brief: Explain why an AI agent is not automatically a neutral employee for its user. Follow the breakout’s simple conflict structure: give an agent a task, introduce competing instructions from the user, employer and model provider, then show how tool access can turn a normal chatbot into something closer to an autonomous worker. Separate the viral claim from the evidence: the concern is about incentives, policies, data access and tested failure modes—not proof that every agent secretly serves its company.

topic_candidates.query: Nvidia Jensen Huang reinstated CEO November 23 2026 board announcement AI chip supply chain
topic_candidates.brief: Explain why Jensen Huang’s reinstatement matters beyond one executive: Nvidia sits near the center of the AI hardware supply chain, so its leadership affects chip strategy, data-center spending and confidence in the AI boom. Tell the story in the breakout’s speculative order: start with the surprising return, trace the political and business pressure around it, then show how GPUs, software ecosystems and national-security concerns make one CEO unusually important. topic_candidates.title: What the TIDAL Ban Really Means
topic_candidates.query: TIDAL ban fully AI-generated music December 9 2026 AI music policy
topic_candidates.brief: Explain what TIDAL is actually banning and what it is not. Begin with the sudden flood of AI-made tracks, then show how a streaming service can use detection and labeling systems, why fully synthetic songs are easier to target than human songs assisted by AI, and what this means for listeners, musicians and other platforms. The key question is whether an AI-music ban can distinguish synthetic production from legitimate tools without false accusations.
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: TIDAL’s policy says that beginning December 9, 2026, wholly AI-generated tracks submitted to the service will be rejected and removed. Reporting says the change follows a rapid increase in AI-generated uploads, while mixed human-and-AI production remains a more complicated category. ([support.tidal.com](https://support.tidal.com/hc/en-us/articles/48031883413521-AI-Policy?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.broke_on: Breakout 8 — “What the Grave Bell Really Meant” by Ricks Clips; 4.5× breakout.
topic_candidates.science_angle: Audio-generation fingerprints, classifier false positives, watermarking and the difference between detecting a fully synthetic signal and detecting AI assistance inside a human recording.

topic_candidates.title: How One Browser Rebuilt Its Entire Engine
topic_candidates.query: Ladybird browser alpha November 23 2026 new browser engine built from scratch
topic_candidates.brief: Use Ladybird’s alpha release to explain what a browser engine actually does. Start with the familiar idea of opening a webpage, then reveal the hidden chain that turns HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels, and explain why building a new engine from scratch is difficult when most of the web depends on a few dominant engines. Make clear that the alpha is an early, crash-prone test rather than a finished replacement for Chrome or Safari.
topic_candidates.evidence_summary: Ladybird announced on November 23, 2026 that its alpha was available for macOS and Linux. The project says its engine is built from the ground up rather than forked from Chromium, Gecko or WebKit, and warns that some sites will not work and crashes are expected. ([ladybird.org](https://ladybird.org/posts/alpha/?utm_source=openai))
topic_candidates.broke_on: Breakout 5 — “How One Cart Stopped an Entire Army” by Ricks Clips; 3.1× breakout.
topic_candidates.science_angle: Browser-engine architecture: parsing, layout, JavaScript execution, rendering, sandboxing and why web standards do not automatically guarantee compatibility.
